title: Trust broken
hook: abuses of power in some Western and Asian centers, and the communities that faced them

segments.voice: Yesterday, women's ordination, and two sides who love the same teacher. Your line: told with respect. Day one thousand forty-five.

The teacher sits on a raised cushion at the front of the hall. Students bow when the teacher enters. The teacher's word on practice is final, and people have rearranged their lives to be near the teacher. Often that trust is a gift; it lets a student go deep. But trust is also power, and power can be misused. Today is uncomfortable, and it belongs in an honest course: what happened when trust was broken in some Buddhist communities, and what they did next.
screen: `A TEACHER ON A RAISED CUSHION.` → `TRUST IS ALSO POWER.` → `WHEN IT WAS BROKEN.`

segments.voice: In some Buddhist centers, in Asia and in the West, teachers have misused the trust placed in them: sexual misconduct with students, bullying, money taken or hidden. People who were harmed have described how hard it was to be heard, because the teacher was respected and the community wanted to protect its practice. Today is about what comes after someone speaks. The Vinaya has a ceremony built for exactly that. At the end of the rains retreat, each monk, the most senior first, faces the others and invites them: about anything they have seen, heard or suspected, speak to me, out of compassion, so I can make amends. It's called the pavarana, the invitation. It takes for granted that anyone, however senior, may need correcting, and it puts that on the calendar. A second teaching is about how to speak. To a prince named Abhaya, the Buddha says he won't say what is false or useless, however welcome. What is true and beneficial he will say even when it's unwelcome, and he knows the right time to say it. True, useful, timed with care. Communities that faced abuse have tried to build both into their life. They listened to the people who were harmed, and took them seriously enough to look. They brought in outside investigators. Some teachers stepped down. Groups wrote ethics codes, named people other than the teacher to receive concerns, and went to the police when a crime was involved. None of it undoes the harm. But it can make the room safer for the next student.
screen: `WHEN TRUST WAS MISUSED.` · `PAVARANA: PLEASE TELL ME.` · `TRUE, USEFUL, AT THE RIGHT TIME.` · then, large: `MAKE THE ROOM SAFER.`

segments.voice: Think of a group you belong to, a center, a congregation, a team, and ask quietly: if something were wrong here, who would I tell besides the person in charge, and is there a written way? If you don't know, notice that without alarm. If someone comes to mind who might need help right now, breathe with that, and know that a trusted person or the local authorities can be called.
Trust broken. When teachers in some Buddhist communities misused their power, and the communities learned to listen, investigate and make things safer. Today's word.
Your line: speak up safely. Anyone, however senior, may need correcting. Day one thousand forty-five, done.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist centers now publish ethics codes, name contacts outside the teacher for raising concerns, and ask outside investigators to look into complaints; Theravada monastic communities hold the pavarana at the end of the rains retreat, inviting one another to point out faults.

chat.says: What did Buddhist communities do when a teacher abused their trust?
options: Listened to those harmed, brought in investigators, wrote ethics codes.
Closed the centers for good and stopped all teaching there.
Nothing; the pavarana forbids students from correcting a teacher.
chat.meaning: They listened to the people harmed, brought in outside investigators, wrote ethics codes, and went to the police when a crime was involved.

pavarana.meaning: the invitation, at the rains' end, for others to name one's faults

rains retreat.meaning: the season monks stay in one place to practice

Abhaya.meaning: a prince the Buddha taught about true, timely speech

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): the draft repeated day 1024 ('How teachers fail') nearly point for point (the same list of abuses, the Vinaya's rules-with-origin-stories, the Kalama Sutta, a near-identical Kalama myth), and the Kalama Sutta returns again on day 1047. Rebuilt the teach on the pavarana (Mahavagga IV: each monk, by seniority, invites correction on what was seen, heard or suspected, out of compassion) and MN 58 (true, beneficial words said even when unwelcome, at the right time). Hook made gender-neutral ('near the teacher'). Games, original (pavarana), trapdoor, sources and howItsDone updated. Older notes below about the Kalama Sutta, 'lay people spoke up' and 'silence was never the Buddha's way' no longer apply.

Editor pass: hook made gender-neutral; 'the code exists because... lay people spoke up' widened to 'people' (complaints come from monks too); the sweeping 'silence was never the Buddha's way' replaced with what the Vinaya stories show.
Deliberately names no teacher, center or lineage. Keeper and owner should confirm this level of generality and the list of harms (sexual misconduct, bullying, money).
Safety: the practice points to 'a trusted person or the local authorities' if someone needs help now; owner may want an in-app resource link on this day.
'The code exists because those in robes did wrong, and lay people spoke up about it': complaints in the Vinaya origin stories often come from lay people but also from monks; confirm the phrasing.
'Silence was never the Buddha's way of handling harm' is an interpretive line; Keeper may soften.
Kalama Sutta paraphrased (no PD translation on the list in hand); confirm the summary of its list of things not to rely on alone.
